prompt.context: Our client is the CEO of a family owned business called GCP, which produces golf clubs in the United States. They used to produce clubs that were easy to use, so most of their customers are beginner players. They recently received a patent for a new club that would enhance the performance of amateurs and professionals alike. Product innovation is paramount in this industry and they want help capitalizing on this development with a strong product launch.
prompt.question: Help GCP plan a strong product launch for their new patented golf club. The interviewer will guide you through several phases: analyzing the market, deciding whether to build a new plant or expand the current one, identifying other relevant issues, identifying risks the CEO faces, and pricing an insurance policy to protect against those risks.

clarifying_info.q: What production methods does GCP currently use?
clarifying_info.a: GCP currently uses liquid production only. Some competitors use solid production.

clarifying_info.q: What is estimated demand for the new club?
clarifying_info.a: We estimate demand for the new club to be 60,000 sets next year.
GCP has contracts to sell 60,000 sets for $500 each.

exhibits.title: Number of Golf Club Sets Sold by Year
exhibits.shows: A chart showing the number of golf club sets sold in 2007, 2008, and estimates for 2009 and the following two years, broken down by market segment (e.g., top 10 liquid producers vs. others).
exhibits.data: Historical data for 2007 and 2008; estimates for 2009 and next two years; market more than doubled over two years; top 10 liquid producers hold a large share of total market.

framework: Analyze market attractiveness: growth rate, market share concentration, competitive dynamics
Capacity decision: evaluate cost of building a new plant vs. expanding current plant to meet 60,000-set demand
Qualitative factors: management/admin, product quality, distribution, risk diversification, future capacity, implementation impact
Risk identification: timing risk and cost overrun risk for the expansion project
Insurance pricing: calculate expected loss to insurer and gross up for margin

questions.prompt: Phase 1 — What do you see in the market chart? Does being a top producer matter?
questions.guidance: The market grew more than 100% in two years, making it highly attractive. The top 10 liquid producers hold a dominant market share. Being at the top matters because top producers likely benefit from economies of scale in production, distribution, and advertising, and are better positioned to invest in product innovation.

questions.prompt: Phase 2 — Given estimated demand of 60,000 sets next year, should GCP build a new additional plant or expand the current plant? (One-time investment of $2M is the same for both options.)
questions.guidance: Compare the machine costs needed to meet 60,000-set annual demand under each option. Ignore the equal $2M one-time investment. For new plant: choose the cheapest combination of up to 3 machine lines that meets 60,000 sets/year. For expansion: choose the cheapest combination of machine lines (no line restriction stated) that meets 60,000 sets/year. Recommend the lower-cost option, and note the costs are nearly equal so qualitative factors matter.

math.setup: New plant machines: Line I = 2,000 sets/month = 24,000/year at $12.5M; Line II = 1,250 sets/month = 15,000/year at $8M; max 3 lines total. Expansion machines: Line I = 1,250 sets/month = 15,000/year at $8M; Line II = 7,500 sets/year at $5.5M; no line limit stated.
steps: New plant option a: 2x Line I + 1x Line II = 24k+24k+15k = 63,000 sets/year; cost = 12.5+12.5+8 = $33M
New plant option b: 3x Line I = 72,000 sets/year; cost = 12.5*3 = $37.5M
New plant best: option a at $33M
Expansion: Line I dominates Line II (15,000/yr vs 7,500/yr; $8M vs $5.5M — Line I is twice output at less than twice cost). Use all Line I machines.
Expansion: need 4 Line I machines: 15,000*4 = 60,000 sets/year; cost = 8*4 = $32M
Comparison: New plant = $33M vs Expansion = $32M — roughly the same ($1M difference)
math.answer: Costs are roughly equal ($33M new plant vs $32M expansion). The $1M difference could be offset by future capacity considerations (new plant has 3,000 extra sets/year capacity). Decision should be made on qualitative factors.

questions.prompt: Phase 3 — Given roughly equal costs, what other issues would you analyze when deciding between the two options? What are the pros and cons of each?
questions.guidance: This is a brainstorm. Strong answers cover multiple dimensions. Push for as many ideas as possible.

questions.prompt: Phase 4 — The CEO decided to expand. What are the two main issues that are keeping the CEO up at night, assuming market estimates are 100% accurate?
questions.guidance: Focus on execution risks for a construction/expansion project: (1) Timing — product innovation is paramount and the market is growing fast, so launching late could mean losing market share; (2) Cost overruns — construction costs may increase after the decision is made, threatening the budget.

questions.prompt: Phase 5 — The CEO wants to buy insurance against those two risks. What do you think the insurance price will be? What information do you need?
questions.guidance: Frame from the insurer's perspective. Calculate expected loss, then gross up for the insurer's margin. Key data: 60,000 sets contracted at $500 each; if GCP produces less than 90% of 60,000 in the next 8 months, they lose 10% of contracts; probability of that event is 20%; insurer operates at 10% margin.

math.setup: Loss event: GCP produces <90% of 60,000 sets → loses 10% of contracts. Loss amount = 10% * 60,000 * $500. Probability of loss = 20%. Insurer margin = 10%, so expected loss = 90% of premium.
steps: Expected loss = 90% of premium (insurer keeps 10% margin)

brainstorming.prompt: What other issues would you want to analyze when deciding between building a new plant vs. expanding the current plant? What are the pros and cons of each option?

categories.name: Management & Administration
ideas: Single plant means lower labor and G&A costs
Easier to enforce consistent management practices and culture

categories.name: Product Quality
ideas: Easier to maintain quality standards with one plant
Two plants introduce risk of quality inconsistency between locations

categories.name: Distribution
ideas: A second plant in a different location could reduce shipping costs to certain markets
Single plant may face higher distribution costs to geographically dispersed customers

categories.name: Risk Diversification
ideas: Two plants diversify event risk (fire, natural disaster, labor strike)
Insurance premiums may be lower with two plants due to lower concentration of assets

categories.name: Future Capacity
ideas: New plant option provides 3,000 extra sets/year of capacity (63k vs 60k) as a buffer for demand growth
Expansion maxes out at exactly 60,000 sets/year with 4 machines

categories.name: Implementation Impact
ideas: Expanding the current plant may disrupt production of existing club lines during construction
Building a separate new plant avoids disruption to current operations

categories.name: Time to Implement
ideas: One option may be faster to build/permit than the other, affecting launch timing
Speed to market is critical given rapid market growth and importance of product innovation

recommendation: Costs of both options are roughly equal (~$32-33M for machines, plus identical $2M one-time investment); qualitative factors should drive the final decision

If preserving current production and launching on time are top priorities, a new plant avoids disruption; if management simplicity and quality control are paramount, expanding the current plant is preferable
risks: Timing risk: expansion construction may delay product launch in a fast-growing market
Cost overrun risk: construction costs may increase after the commitment is made
Demand risk: 60,000-set estimate may be inaccurate; new plant provides a small capacity buffer
next_steps: Obtain fixed-price construction contracts to manage cost overrun risk
Develop a detailed project timeline to ensure launch aligns with market window
Evaluate insurance options — estimated premium ~$667K — to protect against contract loss if production targets are missed
Assess whether future demand growth warrants the additional capacity of the new plant option
